data.title: Declaration merging
data.subtitle: Interface merge, module/global augmentation, Nest Request.user

cards.meaning: TypeScript combines multiple declarations that share the same name into one definition. The most common case: two interface declarations with the same name in the same scope become one interface with all members. You use it on purpose (augmentation) to extend types you do not own — Express Request, library Config, Window — without editing node_modules.

cards.front: What is the result of two interface User { ... } in the same scope?
cards.meaning: Same name and kind (interface) plus compatible members merge into one interface. Later declarations add properties or methods. Conflicting same-name properties with incompatible types error.
cards.example: interface User { id: string } interface User { email: string } // { id: string; email: string }

cards.front: Can type aliases merge or be augmented?
cards.meaning: No — duplicate type alias names are compile errors (Duplicate identifier). If a library exports type Config, you generally cannot reopen it. Augmentation targets must be mergeable interfaces. Library authors often expose interface for config and request shapes so apps can augment.
cards.example: type A = { id: string }; type A = { email: string }; // Error

cards.front: Why do libraries export interface for Config?
cards.meaning: So consumers can module-augment and add fields without forking types. Type aliases for config block reopen-and-merge patterns and force intersection wrappers or a library redesign.

cards.front: Does merging set req.user at runtime?
cards.meaning: No — merging is compile-time only. It does not change runtime objects. Middleware or guards must still assign req.user; types can lie if you forget runtime behavior. Erasure means types do not attach runtime properties.

cards.front: What does declare module 'some-library' { interface Config } do?
cards.meaning: It opens that module's type scope. An interface with the same name as an existing interface in that module merges. The target must be a mergeable interface, not a closed type alias. A side-effect import (import 'some-library') helps the augmentation attach to the library module.
cards.example: declare module 'some-library' { interface Config { myCustomOption?: boolean } }

cards.front: What happens if the declare module string is wrong?
cards.meaning: Silent failure: you get your own local interface that never merges with the library. Wrong target — augmenting 'express' versus the actual namespace or module that defines Request — is the same class of bug. Express Request historically lives under namespace Express / @types/express; the Nest curriculum example uses global namespace Express.

cards.front: How do you type req.user on Express Request (Nest)?
cards.meaning: Declaration merging via global augmentation: a .d.ts with declare global { namespace Express { interface Request { user?: User } } } export {}. TypeScript merges into @types/express Request. Purely compile-time; middleware or a guard must still assign req.user. Do not patch node_modules types.
cards.example: declare global { namespace Express { interface Request { user?: User } } } export {};

cards.front: Why is declare global needed in a file with import or export?
cards.meaning: A file with top-level import or export is a module, so declarations are not global by default. Skipping declare global leaves them module-scoped and they never merge with Express.Request. export {} forces 'this file is a module' so you do not accidentally create a script; pair it with declare global when you still need global merges.
Global augmentation of interface Window inside declare global, then export {}. After that, window.__APP_CONFIG__ type-checks. Same mechanism as Express Request, applied to DOM globals.
cards.example: declare global { interface Window { __APP_CONFIG__?: { apiUrl: string } } } export {};

cards.meaning: Prefer user?: User if unauthenticated requests exist. Required user on all Request references is noisy if many routes are public. Use a narrower typed request or an assertion after auth when you want user required on protected handlers.

cards.front: Augmentation not working — what is a common fix?
cards.meaning: Ensure the .d.ts is part of the compilation — tsconfig include or project references, e.g. include: ["src/**/*", "types/**/*.d.ts"]. Otherwise property user does not exist on Request forever despite correct augmentation code.

cards.front: Request & { user: User } vs augmentation — which updates every Request?
cards.meaning: Intersection is local only; it will not update every Request reference. Augment a third-party interface when you need the same type name everywhere (Request, Config). Augmentation wins when the ecosystem already types many APIs as Request and you want one consistent extension.

cards.front: Is putting everything on Request the only Nest option?
cards.meaning: No. A wrapper type or Nest @CurrentUser() decorator is often cleaner than putting everything on Request. Use augmentation when you truly need the shared Request name; otherwise prefer a dedicated parameter decorator.

cards.front: What happens if you declare interface Request { user } in a random .ts file?
cards.meaning: You create a different Request unless you augment the scope Express actually uses. A local interface does not merge with Express's global Request.

cards.front: Is declaration merging only for interfaces?
cards.meaning: No. Value and namespace combinations exist — function, class, and enum plus namespace (e.g. createApp.Options, Color.isWarm). Interview depth is knowing that; day-to-day Nest/Express work is almost always interface merging via augmentation.
